```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(dar)
set.seed(130)
```

`add_model()` defines one statistical design shared by every compatible
differential-abundance step. Its `targets` and `tax_level` arguments are the
single source of truth for the analysis configuration; other fixed terms provide
covariate adjustment. Method-specific thresholds, normalization and rarefaction
settings remain active. A model-free recipe remains valid for preprocessing,
but differential-abundance execution without a model is deprecated.

## Small example data

These simulated counts illustrate model configuration, not biological findings,
statistical performance or power. There are 12 subjects, each measured at three
visits. The cross-sectional example uses only their baseline samples. Messages
and warnings remain visible; this small example does not establish estimation
quality or validate a method's assumptions.

```{r example-data}
metadata <- expand.grid(
  visit = 0:2, subject_index = 1:6,
  condition = c("control", "treated"),
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
metadata$subject <- paste(metadata$condition, metadata$subject_index, sep = "_")
metadata$batch <- factor(ifelse(metadata$subject_index %% 2 == 0, "A", "B"))
metadata$age <- rep(c(25, 42, 31, 56, 38, 49), each = 3, times = 2)
rownames(metadata) <- paste(metadata$subject, metadata$visit, sep = "_")
means <- outer(seq(40, 150, length.out = 12), rep(1, nrow(metadata)))
means[1, ] <- means[1, ] * ifelse(metadata$condition == "treated", 2, 1)
means[2, ] <- means[2, ] * exp(
  0.3 * metadata$visit * (metadata$condition == "treated")
)
counts <- matrix(
  rnbinom(length(means), mu = as.vector(means), size = 20),
  nrow = nrow(means),
  dimnames = list(paste0("taxon_", seq_len(nrow(means))), rownames(metadata))
)
taxonomy <- cbind(
  Genus = paste0("Genus_", seq_len(nrow(counts))),
  Species = paste0("Species_", seq_len(nrow(counts)))
)
rownames(taxonomy) <- rownames(counts)
longitudinal_phy <- phyloseq::phyloseq(
  phyloseq::otu_table(counts, taxa_are_rows = TRUE),
  phyloseq::tax_table(taxonomy),
  phyloseq::sample_data(metadata)
)
phy <- phyloseq::prune_samples(metadata$visit == 0, longitudinal_phy)
```

## Cross-sectional adjustment

```{r cross-sectional}
rec <- recipe(phy) |>
  add_model(
    ~ condition + batch + age,
    targets = "condition",
    tax_level = "Species",
    reference = c(condition = "control"),
    na_action = "error"
  ) |>
  step_deseq()

get_model(rec)
cross_sectional_fit <- prep(rec, parallel = FALSE)
```

The reference is the denominator, so a positive effect for
`condition[treated-control]` means higher abundance in `treated`. With
`na_action = "drop"`, `prep()` removes one common complete-case cohort before
any engine runs and records the sample identifiers in the execution manifest.
Use `na_action = "error"` when missing model variables should stop the analysis
instead of changing the cohort.

## Longitudinal adjustment

Numeric time values are converted internally to a factor whose levels are
sorted by numeric value. The original sample metadata are not modified.

```{r longitudinal}
longitudinal <- recipe(longitudinal_phy) |>
  add_model(
    ~ condition * visit + batch + (1 | subject),
    targets = "condition",
    tax_level = "Species",
    time = "visit",
    reference = c(condition = "control", visit = "0"),
    contrasts = "all",
    na_action = "drop"
  ) |>
  step_linda()

fit <- prep(longitudinal, parallel = FALSE)
tidy_results(fit) |>
  dplyr::distinct(contrast_id, comparison, contrast_type)
```

For `condition * visit`, the simple plan contains condition comparisons within
every visit and all pairwise visit comparisons within every condition. Later
time values are numerators. `contrasts = "all"` additionally requests
difference-in-differences. More than 12 time points requires an explicit larger
`max_time_levels`, preventing accidental contrast explosions.

`(1 | subject)` specifies a subject-level random intercept for repeated
measurements. Declaring `time` does not itself add a random effect or establish
that observations are independent. Include the subject structure required by
the study design and choose a compatible method.

## Engine capabilities

| Engine | Fixed adjustment | Time interaction | Random effects |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| DESeq2 | yes | yes | no |
| ALDEx2 | yes | yes | no |
| ANCOM-BC2 | yes | yes | yes |
| corncob | yes | yes | no |
| LinDA | yes | yes | yes |
| MaAsLin3 | yes | yes | yes |
| Wilcoxon | no | no | no |
| LEfSe | no | no | no |

Fixed adjustment includes an additive time term, even when that column is
declared with `time`. Wilcoxon and LEfSe support one categorical target without
adjustment; they cannot execute `~ condition + time` with `targets = "condition"`.

Incompatible steps are warned about when the chain is built and rechecked
after preprocessing. `prep()` records them rather than treating them as failed
fits. If no method is compatible, preparation stops. Real engine failures and
missing planned contrasts remain errors.

Use `contrast_id`, `comparison` and `contrast_type` to identify the hypothesis
represented by each result. See
[Getting started with dar](dar.html) for extracting results, inspecting
execution records and plotting selected contrasts.

## Interpret returned results

`tidy_results()` returns one row per returned taxon, contrast and configured
step, not a complete grid of all possible tests. `method` identifies the engine
and `step_id` identifies its configuration. Custom IDs must not collide with
internal columns such as `effect`, `taxa_id` or `sum`; choose distinct IDs such
as `linda_sensitivity`.

The numerator and denominator define each contrast's orientation. Positive
effects point toward the numerator on the reported metric, but the metrics
are not numerically interchangeable:

| Engine | Effect reported by the centralized API |
|:--|:--|
| DESeq2 | Log2 fold change, with the configured shrinkage. |
| ALDEx2 | Contrast-oriented GLM coefficient. |
| ANCOM-BC2 | Bias-corrected log fold change. |
| corncob | Logit mean-abundance coefficient. |
| LinDA | Bias-corrected log2 fold change. |
| MaAsLin3 | Coefficient on the configured transformed abundance scale. |
| Wilcoxon | Difference in medians on the configured abundance scale. |
| LEfSe | Direction-oriented LDA score. |

Inspect `effect_metric` and the configured engine options before interpreting
an estimate. `significant` preserves the originating method's decision,
including any additional criteria such as ANCOM-BC2's pseudocount-sensitivity
filter. Missing statistics remain missing: a nonsignificant result does not
prove that every estimate was available or that there is no effect. Absent
rows are not automatically nonsignificant results. Agreement plots do not
establish calibrated false-discovery rates.

For centralized ALDEx2 analyses, `effect` is the contrast-oriented coefficient
from the same GLM as the adjusted P value, averaged over Monte Carlo instances
and labeled `aldex_glm_coefficient`. With default settings it is on the base-2
CLR response scale, not an absolute-abundance fold change or ALDEx2's
standardized two-group effect. Advanced native settings can change its scale.
Recompute previously prepared centralized ALDEx2 results to obtain the GLM
coefficients; deprecated model-free analyses retain their standardized effects.

## Advanced native-engine arguments

The eight DA steps accept `engine_args`, a named list grouped by native-call
stage. This keeps advanced settings attached to the configured step and avoids
an ambiguous `...`. For example:

```{r engine-args}
advanced <- recipe(phy) |>
  add_model(
    ~ condition + batch + age, targets = "condition", tax_level = "Species",
    reference = c(condition = "control")
  ) |>
  step_deseq(
    engine_args = list(
      fit = list(minReplicatesForReplace = Inf),
      shrink = list(lfcThreshold = 1)
    )
  ) |>
  step_ancom(
    engine_args = list(
      fit = list(iter_control = list(tol = 1e-3, max_iter = 50, verbose = FALSE))
    )
  )
advanced
```

Nested native control lists replace the corresponding native argument; they
are not merged with its defaults. For ANCOM-BC2, supply the complete
`iter_control` list, including `verbose`, rather than only the values changed.

Available stages are `size_factors`, `fit`, `results`, and `shrink` for
DESeq2; `clr` and `fit` for ALDEx2; `fit` for ANCOM-BC2,
corncob, and LinDA; `fit` and `contrast` for MaAsLin3; `test` for Wilcoxon;
and `transform` and `fit` for LEfSe. Data, formulas, contrasts, output paths
and arguments already exposed by each dar wrapper are protected. Non-empty
`engine_args` require a centralized model. A configured stage that is not
used by the selected execution route is reported as an error.
ALDEx2's former `effect` stage is rejected because centralized effects now
come directly from the GLM fit.

See [Saving and sharing analysis recipes](import_export_recipes.html) for
exporting model settings and native options without executing an analysis.

## Migrating legacy selectors

The former `recipe(..., var_info=, tax_info=)`, `add_var()`, `add_tax()`,
`get_var()` and `get_tax()` interfaces, and model-free DA execution, are
deprecated in Bioconductor 3.24, become defunct in 3.25 and are scheduled for
removal in 3.26. Preprocessing without a model remains supported. Move the
selectors into `add_model()` and inspect them with `get_model(rec)`:

```{r migration, eval=FALSE}
# Deprecated
old <- recipe(phy, var_info = "condition", tax_info = "Species")

# Current API
current <- recipe(phy) |>
  add_model(
    ~ condition,
    targets = "condition",
    tax_level = "Species"
  )
```

`phy_qc()` is defunct in 3.24; use `recipe_qc()`. The retired
`step_metagenomeseq()` is no longer exported. Legacy executable recipe files
must be recreated in the current API before export; they are not accepted by
the current importer.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
